Two regimes that ruled Egypt, and usually Syria, from 1171 to 1517. First came the Ayyubid family of Saladin, then the Mamluks, a caste of slave soldiers who made themselves sultans.

The Ayyubids (1171 to 1250). Saladin, a Kurdish officer, ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171. He united Egypt and Syria and retook Jerusalem from the crusaders in 1187. His relatives split his lands after his death. They bought Turkish boys from the steppe, trained them as soldiers and freed them. These were the mamluks.

The Mamluks (1250 to 1517). In 1250, during a crusade led by Louis IX of France, the mamluks killed the last Ayyubid sultan and took power. Ten years later they beat the Mongols at Ain Jalut, the first real check on Mongol expansion. Sultan Baybars and his successors then took the last crusader cities, ending with Acre in 1291. They kept a line of Abbasid caliphs in Cairo to lend them legitimacy.

Cairo was the largest city of the Muslim world. Spices from India came up the Red Sea and on to Venice, and the sultans taxed them. Mansa Musa passed through in 1324 and spent so much gold that its price fell. Ibn Khaldun spent his last years there as a judge.

The Black Death from 1347 hit Egypt hard. Later, Portuguese ships sailing round Africa cut into the spice trade. In 1517 the Ottomans conquered Egypt, though mamluk households kept local power for three more centuries.
sum: Two regimes that ruled Egypt, and usually Syria, from 1171 to 1517. First came the Ayyubid family of Saladin, then the Mamluks, a caste of slave soldiers who made themselves sultans.
